claim: CAPERα was identified in anti-TBX3 immunoprecipitated proteins from HEK293 cell lysates by mass spectrometry.
source: Among these, mass spectrometry of anti-TBX3 immunoprecipitated (IP'd) proteins identified CAPERα (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1A, which displays a representative spectrum for CAPERα with six specific peptides providing 8.5% sequence coverage.

claim: Tbx3 and Caperα interact in vivo in e10.5 mouse embryos.
source: To determine if Tbx3 and Caperα interact in vivo, we IP'd endogenous Caperα from embryonic day (e)10.5 mouse embryo lysates (Figure 1B). Immunoblotting for Tbx3 confirmed its interaction with Caperα (Figure 1C, lane 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments from mouse embryo lysates shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The interaction between Caperα and Tbx3 is direct.
source: in vitro pull down assays revealed that their interaction is direct (Figure 1D, lane 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro MBP pull down assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Tbx3 and Caperα proteins are co-expressed in mouse embryonic dorsal root ganglia at e10.5.
source: Immunohistochemistry on sectioned e10.5 embryos showed that Tbx3 and Caperα proteins are co-expressed and have distinct localization patterns in different tissues: Caperα is detected in all dorsal root ganglia nuclei (Figure 1E), some of which contain co-localized Tbx3
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In proximal limb mesenchyme, Tbx3 and Caperα co-localize in nuclei.
source: in proximal limb mesenchyme, Tbx3 and Caperα co-localize in nuclei (Figure 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In some distal limb cells and ectoderm, Caperα is nuclear and Tbx3 is cytoplasmic.
source: while in some distal cells and the ectoderm, Caperα is nuclear and Tbx3 is cytoplasmic (Figure 1G, white arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The DNA binding domain of Tbx3 is not required for interaction with CAPERα.
source: Immunoblot of anti-CAPERα IP'd samples shows that the endogenous CAPERα interacts with Tbx3 DBD mutant proteins (Figure 1J′, lanes 2 and 3 are L143P and N227D, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing that DBD point mutants still interact with CAPERα, as shown in Figure 1J′.

claim: Deletions of the Tbx3 C-terminus more proximal than amino acid 655 disrupt the CAPERα/Tbx3 interaction.
source: Myc-tagged deletion mutants are IP'd by the anti-Myc antibody (Figure 1K), and probing anti-Myc IP'd material for CAPERα reveals that deletions more proximal than amino acid 655 disrupt the CAPERα/Tbx3 interaction (Figure 1K′).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with C-terminal deletion mutants shown in Figures 1K and 1K′.

claim: The C-terminal repressor domain of Tbx3 is required for interaction with CAPERα.
source: Although the untagged ΔRD mutant is produced in TBX3 shRNA knockdown cells and IP'd by the anti-Tbx3 antibody (Figure 1L and Kumar et al., 2014) it does not interact with CAPERα (Figure 1L′).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing that deletion of the repressor domain prevents CAPERα interaction, as shown in Figure 1L′.

claim: A C-terminal Tbx3 frameshift mutant similar to one identified in humans with UMS does not interact with CAPERα.
source: CAPERα also fails to interact with a C-terminal Tbx3 frameshift mutant similar to one identified in humans with UMS (Bamshad et al., 1999) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of TBX3 in primary human foreskin fibroblasts results in increased senescence associated β-galactosidase activity.
source: Knockdown of either protein resulted in a dramatic increase in senescence associated β-galatosidase activity (SA-βgal, Figure 2A–D; Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2C–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 2A-D and supplementary figures.

claim: Knockdown of CAPERα in primary human foreskin fibroblasts results in increased senescence associated β-galactosidase activity.
source: Knockdown of either protein resulted in a dramatic increase in senescence associated β-galatosidase activity (SA-βgal, Figure 2A–D; Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2C–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 2A-D and supplementary figures.

claim: The senescence phenotype caused by TBX3 knockdown is specific and can be rescued by overexpression of Tbx3.
source: This effect is specific because it occurs with two different shRNAs and is rescued by overexpression of CAPERα (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,E,G,H) and Tbx3 (Figure2—figure supplement 2B,E,G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The senescence phenotype caused by CAPERα knockdown is specific and can be rescued by overexpression of CAPERα.
source: This effect is specific because it occurs with two different shRNAs and is rescued by overexpression of CAPERα (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,E,G,H) and Tbx3 (Figure2—figure supplement 2B,E,G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of TBX3 or CAPERα in HFFs results in formation of senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHFs).
source: Consistent with this, both KDs dramatically influenced nuclear structure, chromatin organization and formation of SAHFs (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of H3K9me3 shown in Figures 2G-J.

claim: Knockdown of TBX3 or CAPERα in HFFs results in evidence of nuclear disruption.
source: Note increased nuclear punctate staining consistent with Senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHFs) in both channels and evidence of nuclear disruption (white arrowheads in red channel) after loss of either TBX3 or CAPERα.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figures 2G-J.

claim: CAPERα and TBX3 knockdown in HFFs results in increased expression of CDKN2A-p16INK.
source: Increased expression of CDKN2A-p16INK (henceforth referred to as p16INK) and decreased PCNA, E2F1 and 2, CDK2, CDK4, CDC2 transcripts indicate that CAPERα/TBX3 represses the p16/RB pathway in proliferating HFFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2K and RT-PCR data in Figures 2L-M.

claim: CAPERα and TBX3 knockdown in HFFs results in decreased expression of PCNA, E2F1, E2F2, CDK2, CDK4, and CDC2.
source: Increased expression of CDKN2A-p16INK (henceforth referred to as p16INK) and decreased PCNA, E2F1 and 2, CDK2, CDK4, CDC2 transcripts indicate that CAPERα/TBX3 represses the p16/RB pathway in proliferating HFFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and RT-PCR data shown in Figures 2K-M.

claim: CAPERα and TBX3 knockdown in HFFs results in increased expression of PMAIP1 and CDKN1A-p21.
source: PMAIP1, CDKN1A-p21, and other p53 pathway members were also increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and RT-PCR data shown in Figures 2K-M.

claim: CAPERα and TBX3 are required to prevent senescence of primary HFFs and act upstream of major cell cycle and senescence regulatory pathways.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that CAPERα and TBX3 are required to prevent senescence of primary HFFs and act upstream of major cell cycle and senescence regulatory pathways.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective data from knockdown experiments showing effects on SA-βgal activity, cell proliferation, nuclear structure, and expression of cell cycle and senescence markers.

claim: Tbx3 null murine embryonic fibroblasts have increased SA-βgal activity compared to wild type MEFs.
source: WT MEFs undergo ∼10 passages with regular, 20 hr doubling times. In contrast, Tbx3−/− MEFs had increased SA-βgal activity and ceased proliferating after only four passages (Figure 2N–Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 2N-P.

claim: Tbx3 null murine embryonic fibroblasts cease proliferating after only four passages.
source: WT MEFs undergo ∼10 passages with regular, 20 hr doubling times. In contrast, Tbx3−/− MEFs had increased SA-βgal activity and ceased proliferating after only four passages (Figure 2N–Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3T5 cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2Q.

claim: Most Tbx3 null MEFs have distorted or ruptured nuclei.
source: Most Tbx3−/− MEFs had distorted or ruptured nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by laminβ1 staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Laminβ1 staining is altered in Tbx3 null MEFs at passage 1.
source: and laminβ1 staining was already altered at passage 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B′).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B′.

claim: Caperα localization is markedly abnormal in Tbx3 null MEFs after only 1 passage.
source: Caperα localization is markedly abnormal in Tbx3−/− MEFS after only 1 passage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D–F′).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D-F′.

claim: Tbx3 is required for preservation of nuclear architecture in proliferating cells.
source: These data suggest that Tbx3 is required for preservation of nuclear architecture and to tether Caperα in its normal nuclear domains in proliferating cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed nuclear distortion and Caperα mislocalization in Tbx3 null MEFs.

claim: Tbx3 is required to tether Caperα in its normal nuclear domains in proliferating cells.
source: These data suggest that Tbx3 is required for preservation of nuclear architecture and to tether Caperα in its normal nuclear domains in proliferating cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed Caperα mislocalization in Tbx3 null MEFs.

claim: In Tbx3 null embryos, RB is hypophosphorylated on multiple serine residues.
source: in protein lysates from Tbx3−/− embryos, RB was hypophosphorylated on multiple serine residues, consistent with increased p16 and decreased Cdk2 and Cdk4 protein levels relative to control (Figure 2R).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2R.

claim: In Tbx3 null embryos, p16 protein levels are increased relative to control.
source: in protein lysates from Tbx3−/− embryos, RB was hypophosphorylated on multiple serine residues, consistent with increased p16 and decreased Cdk2 and Cdk4 protein levels relative to control (Figure 2R).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2R.

claim: In Tbx3 null embryos, Cdk2 and Cdk4 protein levels are decreased relative to control.
source: in protein lysates from Tbx3−/− embryos, RB was hypophosphorylated on multiple serine residues, consistent with increased p16 and decreased Cdk2 and Cdk4 protein levels relative to control (Figure 2R).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2R.

claim: In Tbx3 null embryos, p21 levels are increased.
source: The levels of p21 and other senescence markers were increased, while numerous Cyclins and other Cdks were decreased (Figure 2R, Figure 2—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2R.

claim: In Tbx3 null embryos, numerous Cyclins and other Cdks are decreased.
source: The levels of p21 and other senescence markers were increased, while numerous Cyclins and other Cdks were decreased (Figure 2R, Figure 2—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and qPCR data shown in Figure 2R and Figure 2—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Tbx3 is required to prevent senescence in embryonic mice and MEFs.
source: All of these findings are consistent with a requirement for Tbx3 to prevent senescence in embryonic mice and MEFs.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective data from Tbx3 null embryos and MEFs showing increased senescence markers and decreased cell cycle promoting factors.

claim: Knockdown of p53 does not rescue SA-βgal activity caused by TBX3 or CAPERα knockdown in HFFs.
source: Surprisingly, although p53 shRNA effectively decreased p53 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), it did not rescue SA-βgal activity or growth arrest due to absence of TBX3 or CAPERα (Figure 3B,E,G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 3B, E, G, and H.

claim: Knockdown of p53 does not rescue growth arrest caused by TBX3 or CAPERα knockdown in HFFs.
source: Surprisingly, although p53 shRNA effectively decreased p53 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), it did not rescue SA-βgal activity or growth arrest due to absence of TBX3 or CAPERα (Figure 3B,E,G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Knockdown of RB rescues SA-βgal activity caused by TBX3 and CAPERα knockdown in HFFs.
source: In contrast, shRNA-mediated KD of either RB (Boehm et al., 2005) or p16 (Haga et al., 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) rescued these phenotypes in TBX3 and CAPERα KD cells (Figure 3C,F–H,I–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 3C, F, G.

claim: Knockdown of p16 rescues SA-βgal activity caused by TBX3 and CAPERα knockdown in HFFs.
source: In contrast, shRNA-mediated KD of either RB (Boehm et al., 2005) or p16 (Haga et al., 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) rescued these phenotypes in TBX3 and CAPERα KD cells (Figure 3C,F–H,I–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 3I-M.

claim: Knockdown of RB rescues growth arrest caused by TBX3 and CAPERα knockdown in HFFs.
source: In contrast, shRNA-mediated KD of either RB (Boehm et al., 2005) or p16 (Haga et al., 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) rescued these phenotypes in TBX3 and CAPERα KD cells (Figure 3C,F–H,I–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Knockdown of p16 rescues growth arrest caused by TBX3 and CAPERα knockdown in HFFs.
source: In contrast, shRNA-mediated KD of either RB (Boehm et al., 2005) or p16 (Haga et al., 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) rescued these phenotypes in TBX3 and CAPERα KD cells (Figure 3C,F–H,I–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3N.

claim: The p16/RB pathway mediates senescence downstream of CAPERα and TBX3 loss-of-function in primary cells.
source: These rescue experiments demonstrate that the p16/RB pathway mediates senescence downstream of CAPERα and TBX3 loss-of-function in primary cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the rescue experiments showing that knockdown of RB or p16, but not p53, rescues senescence phenotypes caused by TBX3 or CAPERα knockdown.

claim: CAPERα and TBX3 bind to three regulatory elements upstream of the CDKN2A-p16INK transcriptional start site in HFFs.
source: We screened 7 amplicons spanning ∼6 kb upstream of p16INK by ChIP-PCR of HFF chromatin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); 3 amplicons were bound by CAPERα and TBX3 (Figure 3O, lanes 7, 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3O and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of TBX3 decreases the heterochromatic mark H3K9me3 at CDKN2A-p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Loss of either protein decreased the heterochromatic marks H3K9me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 14, 15) and H3K27me3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and increased the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 17, 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: Loss of CAPERα decreases the heterochromatic mark H3K9me3 at CDKN2A-p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Loss of either protein decreased the heterochromatic marks H3K9me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 14, 15) and H3K27me3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and increased the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 17, 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: Loss of TBX3 decreases the heterochromatic mark H3K27me3 at CDKN2A-p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Loss of either protein decreased the heterochromatic marks H3K9me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 14, 15) and H3K27me3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and increased the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 17, 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Loss of CAPERα decreases the heterochromatic mark H3K27me3 at CDKN2A-p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Loss of either protein decreased the heterochromatic marks H3K9me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 14, 15) and H3K27me3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and increased the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 17, 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Loss of TBX3 increases the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 at CDKN2A-p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Loss of either protein decreased the heterochromatic marks H3K9me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 14, 15) and H3K27me3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and increased the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 17, 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: Loss of CAPERα increases the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 at CDKN2A-p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Loss of either protein decreased the heterochromatic marks H3K9me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 14, 15) and H3K27me3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and increased the euchromatic mark H3K4me3 (Figure 3O, lanes 17, 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: TBX3 knockdown decreases CAPERα occupancy of p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Notably, less CAPERα occupied p16INK elements after TBX3 KD (Figure 3O, lanes 11) while the amount of TBX3 bound post-CAPERα KD was comparable to control (Figure 3O, lanes 9 vs 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: CAPERα knockdown does not significantly affect TBX3 occupancy of p16INK regulatory elements.
source: Notably, less CAPERα occupied p16INK elements after TBX3 KD (Figure 3O, lanes 11) while the amount of TBX3 bound post-CAPERα KD was comparable to control (Figure 3O, lanes 9 vs 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: CAPERα requires TBX3 to occupy p16INK regulatory chromatin.
source: This is consistent with the abnormal localization of CAPERα seen in Tbx3−/− MEFS (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D′–F′) and indicates that CAPERα requires TBX3 to occupy p16INK regulatory chromatin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TBX3 knockdown decreases CAPERα binding to p16INK elements, while CAPERα knockdown does not affect TBX3 binding.

claim: TBX3 and CAPERα associate with the p14ARF initiator.
source: Antibodies against TBX3 and CAPERα ChIP'd the p14ARF initiator (Lingbeek et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: TBX3 knockdown disrupts CAPERα binding to the p14ARF initiator.
source: here too, TBX3 KD disrupted CAPERα binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A′, red arrowhead).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A′.

claim: Neither CAPERα nor TBX3 associate with amplicons scanning 1.8 kb upstream of CDKN1A-p21.
source: Neither CAPERα nor TBX3 associated with amplicons scanning 1.8 kb upstream of CDKN1A-p21 or elements reportedly bound by TBX2 or TBX3 in other cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) (Prince et al., 2004; Saramaki et al., 2006; Hoogaars et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Neither CAPERα nor TBX3 associate with known regulatory elements of CDK2, CDK4, or CDKN1B.
source: Testing for association with known regulatory elements of CDK2, CDK4, CDKN1B was also negative (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C–E) (Baksh et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2005; Louie et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C-E.

claim: In proliferating primary cells, CAPERα/TBX3 specifically and directly represses the CDKN2A locus by binding multiple regulatory sequence elements and regulating chromatin marks.
source: These data indicate that in proliferating primary cells, CAPERα/TBX3 specifically and directly repress the CDKN2A locus by binding multiple regulatory sequence elements and regulating chromatin marks.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the ChIP-PCR data showing CAPERα/TBX3 binding to CDKN2A regulatory elements and changes in chromatin marks upon knockdown.

claim: DUSP4 transcripts are upregulated in response to knockdown of TBX3 and CAPERα in HEK293 cells.
source: Although most transcripts were unaffected by either KD, or changes were not shared (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), DUSP4 and UCA1 were upregulated (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential display data shown in Figure 4D and validated by RT-PCR in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: UCA1 transcripts are upregulated in response to knockdown of TBX3 and CAPERα in HEK293 cells.
source: Although most transcripts were unaffected by either KD, or changes were not shared (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), DUSP4 and UCA1 were upregulated (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential display data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DUSP4 overexpression induces senescence downstream of RB/E2F.
source: DUSP4 is known to regulate cell survival and tumor progression, and overexpression induces senescence downstream of RB/E2F (Torres et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Knockdown of CAPERα or TBX3 in primary HFFs increases UCA1 transcript levels.
source: We found that shRNA KD of CAPERα or TBX3 in primary HFFS recapitulated the increase in UCA1 transcripts seen in HEK293 cells (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR and qPCR data shown in Figures 4E-H.

claim: TBX3 and CAPERα bind to region A3 upstream of the UCA1 gene in HFFs.
source: We assayed 3 amplicons in this region (Figure 4I: A1, A2, A3) by ChIP-PCR of TBX3 and CAPERα: only region A3 was bound (Figure 4J,K, lanes 18, red arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figures 4J and 4K.

claim: TBX3 knockdown results in loss of repressive chromatin marks H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 on UCA1/A3.
source: After TBX3 KD, activating chromatin marks replaced repressive ones (Figure 4L, lanes 13, 15 and 19)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: TBX3 knockdown results in gain of activating chromatin mark H3K4me3 on UCA1/A3.
source: After TBX3 KD, activating chromatin marks replaced repressive ones (Figure 4L, lanes 13, 15 and 19)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: TBX3 knockdown decreases CAPERα binding to UCA1/A3.
source: After TBX3 KD, activating chromatin marks replaced repressive ones (Figure 4L, lanes 13, 15 and 19) and markedly less CAPERα was bound (Figure 4L, lane 17, red arrowhead).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: CAPERα knockdown results in loss of repressive chromatin marks on UCA1/A3.
source: CAPERα KD also led to loss of repressive marks on UCA1/A3 (Figure 4M lanes 9, 16)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: CAPERα knockdown does not prevent TBX3 binding to UCA1/A3.
source: although TBX3 remained bound (Figure 4M, lane 11, red arrowhead).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: TBX3 recruits CAPERα to UCA1/A3 chromatin.
source: Combined with previous findings, we conclude that: (1) TBX3 recruits CAPERα to UCA1/A3 chromatin
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TBX3 knockdown decreases CAPERα binding to UCA1/A3, while CAPERα knockdown does not affect TBX3 binding.

claim: TBX3 alone is insufficient to repress UCA1.
source: (2) TBX3 alone is insufficient to repress UCA1
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CAPERα knockdown leads to loss of repressive marks on UCA1/A3 even though TBX3 remains bound.

claim: The default state of UCA1 in proliferating HFFs is repression conferred by CAPERα/TBX3.
source: and, (3) the default state of UCA1 in proliferating HFFs is repression conferred by CAPERα/TBX3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that knockdown of either CAPERα or TBX3 leads to increased UCA1 expression.

claim: Overexpression of UCA1 in HFFs results in a robust SA-βgal response 4 days after transfection.
source: UCA1 transcripts are low in proliferating HFFs, but 4 days after overexpression of UCA1 (Figure 5A), a robust SA-βgal response is evident (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: Cells constitutively expressing UCA1 cease proliferating during selection.
source: Cells constitutively expressing UCA1 ceased proliferating during selection and accumulated SAHFs (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Cells constitutively expressing UCA1 accumulate SAHFs.
source: Cells constitutively expressing UCA1 ceased proliferating during selection and accumulated SAHFs (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Cell proliferation decreases in a UCA1 dosage-sensitive manner.
source: Cell proliferation decreased in a UCA1 dosage-sensitive manner (Figure 5G–I)
evidence: The claim is supported by cell count and crystal violet assay data shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: UCA1 overexpression in HFFs results in decreased levels of cell cycle promoting transcripts.
source: consistent with reduced levels of cell cycle promoting transcripts and increased levels of pro-senescence ones (Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: UCA1 overexpression in HFFs results in increased levels of pro-senescence transcripts.
source: consistent with reduced levels of cell cycle promoting transcripts and increased levels of pro-senescence ones (Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Transcriptional changes caused by UCA1 overexpression are manifest at the protein level.
source: These transcriptional changes were manifest at the protein level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of UCA1 in HFFs induces premature senescence.
source: Premature senescence resulting from overexpression of UCA1 in HFFs reveals that this lncRNA is a novel regulator of cell proliferation and may function as a tumor suppressor in some contexts.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective data showing that UCA1 overexpression induces SA-βgal activity, SAHFs, decreased proliferation, and changes in cell cycle and senescence markers.

claim: UCA1 is a novel regulator of cell proliferation.
source: Premature senescence resulting from overexpression of UCA1 in HFFs reveals that this lncRNA is a novel regulator of cell proliferation and may function as a tumor suppressor in some contexts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that UCA1 overexpression induces senescence and affects cell cycle gene expression.

claim: UCA1 may function as a tumor suppressor in some contexts.
source: Premature senescence resulting from overexpression of UCA1 in HFFs reveals that this lncRNA is a novel regulator of cell proliferation and may function as a tumor suppressor in some contexts.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that UCA1 induces senescence, which is a tumor suppressor mechanism.

claim: UCA1 transcript levels are markedly higher in RAS HFFs compared to presenescent HFFs.
source: There are markedly more UCA1 transcripts in RAS compared to presenescent 'PS' HFFs (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Knockdown of UCA1 in RAS HFFs reduces SA-βgal activity.
source: Knockdown of UCA1 in RAS HFFs reduced SA-βgal activity (Figure 5L–Q)
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-βgal assay data shown in Figures 5L-Q.

claim: Knockdown of UCA1 in RAS HFFs improves cell growth.
source: and improved RAS cell growth: the number of Ki67 + RAS cells was increased at days 3 and 6 after UCA1 KD (Figure 5R, P0 and P1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 5R.

claim: By passage 2, the number of Ki67+ cells in UCA1 knockdown RAS HFFs is not statistically different from control despite persistently low levels of UCA1.
source: However, by passage 2, the number of Ki67 + cells was not statistically different in UCA1 KD cells from control, despite persistently low levels of UCA1 (Figure 5S)
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 5R and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5S.

claim: Senescence can occur in the absence of high levels of UCA1.
source: Overall, this indicates that senescence can occur in the absence of high levels of UCA1 but that timely execution of the OIS program requires UCA1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that UCA1 knockdown delays but does not prevent senescence in RAS HFFs.

claim: Timely execution of the OIS program requires UCA1.
source: Overall, this indicates that senescence can occur in the absence of high levels of UCA1 but that timely execution of the OIS program requires UCA1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that UCA1 knockdown delays senescence in RAS HFFs.

claim: The CAPERα/TBX3 repressor dissociates from UCA1/A3 in RAS HFFs.
source: Indeed, the repressor dissociates from UCA1/A3 in RAS HFFs and UCA1/A3 chromatin switches from heterochromatic to euchromatic marks (Figure 5U).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5U.

claim: UCA1/A3 chromatin switches from heterochromatic to euchromatic marks in RAS HFFs.
source: Indeed, the repressor dissociates from UCA1/A3 in RAS HFFs and UCA1/A3 chromatin switches from heterochromatic to euchromatic marks (Figure 5U).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5U.

claim: CAPERα/TBX3 regulation of UCA1 occurs in oncogene-induced senescence.
source: This is consistent with the senescence-inducing effects of CAPERα/TBX3 loss-of-function (Figure 2) and resulting upregulation of UCA1 (Figure 4), and establishes CAPERα/TBX3 regulation of UCA1 in an independent model of senescence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CAPERα/TBX3 dissociates from UCA1/A3 in RAS-induced senescence, similar to what occurs with CAPERα/TBX3 knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of UCA1 results in stabilization of mature p16INK mRNA.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of UCA1 resulted in the stabilization of mature p16INK, p14ARF, E2F1, and TGFβ1 mRNAs: in the time frame examined, p16INK, p14ARF, and E2F1 mRNAs do not decay and their t1/2 values are therefore denoted as 'n' (no decay).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of UCA1 results in stabilization of mature p14ARF mRNA.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of UCA1 resulted in the stabilization of mature p16INK, p14ARF, E2F1, and TGFβ1 mRNAs: in the time frame examined, p16INK, p14ARF, and E2F1 mRNAs do not decay and their t1/2 values are therefore denoted as 'n' (no decay).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of UCA1 results in stabilization of mature E2F1 mRNA.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of UCA1 resulted in the stabilization of mature p16INK, p14ARF, E2F1, and TGFβ1 mRNAs: in the time frame examined, p16INK, p14ARF, and E2F1 mRNAs do not decay and their t1/2 values are therefore denoted as 'n' (no decay).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of UCA1 results in stabilization of mature TGFβ1 mRNA.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of UCA1 resulted in the stabilization of mature p16INK, p14ARF, E2F1, and TGFβ1 mRNAs: in the time frame examined, p16INK, p14ARF, and E2F1 mRNAs do not decay and their t1/2 values are therefore denoted as 'n' (no decay). The half-life estimates shown were calculated using linear regression; those best fit lines, their equations and R values are shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. t1/2 of p16INK mRNA in control cells was 3.9 hr vs n in UCA1 overexpressing cells; p14ARF, 2.4 vs n; E2F1, 7.2 vs n; TGFβ1, 1.9 vs 2.9.
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UCA1 overexpression does not affect the decay rates of MYC, CDKN1A-p21, CDKN2D, and RB mRNAs.
source: In marked contrast, MYC, CDKN1A-p21, CDKN2D and RB mRNAs decayed at rates indistinguishable from control (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of UCA1 overexpression on p16INK mRNA stability were confirmed by Northern blot.
source: The effects of UCA1 overexpression on p16INK mRNA stability were confirmed by Northern blot (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of hnRNP A1 stabilizes p16INK mRNA.
source: To this end, we treated HFFs with siRNA to hnRNP A1 and used Actinomycin D to assess stability of p16INK transcripts. Loss of hnRNP A1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) stabilized both p16INK (t1/2–2.1 in control vs 12.3 after HNRNP A1 knockdown) and p14ARF mRNAs (t1/2–1.5 in control vs 6.9 after hnRNP A1 knockdown) but not those of E2F1 or MYC (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of hnRNP A1 stabilizes p14ARF mRNA.
source: Loss of hnRNP A1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) stabilized both p16INK (t1/2–2.1 in control vs 12.3 after HNRNP A1 knockdown) and p14ARF mRNAs (t1/2–1.5 in control vs 6.9 after hnRNP A1 knockdown) but not those of E2F1 or MYC (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of hnRNP A1 does not affect the stability of E2F1 or MYC mRNAs.
source: Loss of hnRNP A1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) stabilized both p16INK (t1/2–2.1 in control vs 12.3 after HNRNP A1 knockdown) and p14ARF mRNAs (t1/2–1.5 in control vs 6.9 after hnRNP A1 knockdown) but not those of E2F1 or MYC (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: hnRNP A1 binds p16INK mRNA in proliferating cells.
source: We next used RNA-IP (RIP) to determine if hnRNP A1 binds p16INK and p14ARF mRNAs in proliferating cells and found that this was indeed the case (Figure 6C, lane 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: hnRNP A1 binds p14ARF mRNA in proliferating cells.
source: We next used RNA-IP (RIP) to determine if hnRNP A1 binds p16INK and p14ARF mRNAs in proliferating cells and found that this was indeed the case (Figure 6C, lane 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: hnRNP A1/p16INK binding is lost in RAS HFFs.
source: Remarkably, hnRNP A1/p16INK binding was lost in RAS HFFs (Figure 6C, lane 7), despite an overall increase in the number of p16INK transcripts (Figure 6C, lane 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: UCA1 RNA levels increase in RAS HFFs.
source: As shown previously, UCA1 RNA levels also increase with RAS (Figure 6D, lane 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: UCA1 is bound by hnRNP A1 in presenescent cells.
source: UCA1 is bound by hnRNP A1 in PS cells (Figure 6D, lanes 6, 7; Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: The hnRNP A1/UCA1 interaction increases in RAS cells.
source: but unlike p16INK, the hnRNP A1/UCA1 interaction increases in RAS cells (Figure 6D, lane 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The interaction between UCA1 and hnRNP A1 is specific.
source: The interaction between UCA1 and hnRNP A1 is specific, as UCA1 does not bind hnRNP K, C1/C2, H, U, or D (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: hnRNP A1 binds MYC mRNA.
source: Although hnRNP A1 binds MYC and p14ARF mRNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: hnRNP A1 does not bind RB, p21, or CDK6 mRNAs under the conditions tested.
source: it does not bind RB, p21 or CDK6 mRNAs under the numerous conditions tested (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: Direct overexpression of UCA1 disrupts the hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction.
source: In control transfected proliferating cells, there is robust binding of p16INK to hnRNP A1 (Figure 6C, lane13), but direct overexpression of UCA1 (Figure 6D, lane 10) or that resulting from TBX3 or CAPERα KD (Figure 6D, lanes 17, 18) disrupts the hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction (Figure 6C, lanes14, 23, 24, red arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: TBX3 knockdown disrupts the hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction.
source: In control transfected proliferating cells, there is robust binding of p16INK to hnRNP A1 (Figure 6C, lane13), but direct overexpression of UCA1 (Figure 6D, lane 10) or that resulting from TBX3 or CAPERα KD (Figure 6D, lanes 17, 18) disrupts the hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction (Figure 6C, lanes14, 23, 24, red arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: CAPERα knockdown disrupts the hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction.
source: In control transfected proliferating cells, there is robust binding of p16INK to hnRNP A1 (Figure 6C, lane13), but direct overexpression of UCA1 (Figure 6D, lane 10) or that resulting from TBX3 or CAPERα KD (Figure 6D, lanes 17, 18) disrupts the hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction (Figure 6C, lanes14, 23, 24, red arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Loss of hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction in OIS is the result of increased UCA1 expression and its binding and sequestration of hnRNP A1.
source: These findings support the hypothesis that loss of hnRNP A1/p16INK mRNA interaction in OIS (Figure 6C, lane 7) is the result of increased UCA1 expression and its binding and sequestration of hnRNP A1 (Figure 6D, lane 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that UCA1 levels increase in OIS, UCA1 binds hnRNP A1, and hnRNP A1/p16INK binding is lost in OIS.

claim: UCA1 knockdown in RAS HFFs restores the interaction between hnRNP A1 and p16INK mRNA.
source: To further test this, we used shRNA to KD UCA1 in RAS HFFs (Figure 6D, lane 27). UCA1 KD restored the interaction between hnRNP A1 and p16INK mRNA (Figure 6C, lane 31)
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: UCA1 knockdown in RAS HFFs leads to lower levels of total p16INK mRNA.
source: and led to lower levels of total p16INK mRNA (Figure 6C, lane 27), a finding consistent with the negative effects of hnRNP A1/ p16INK interaction on stability of p16INK transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The effects of UCA1 on p16INK mRNA stability are specific.
source: The effects of UCA1 on p16INK mRNA stability are specific, because hnRNP A1 interactions with MYC or p14ARF mRNAs are unaffected by UCA1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4 (note: the text references 'Figure 6—figure supplement 1' but this appears to be an error and should be 'Figure 6—figure supplement 4').

claim: In proliferating cells, the very low quantity of UCA1 transcripts is insufficient to disrupt hnRNP A1/p16INK binding.
source: In total, these findings indicate that in proliferating cells, the very low quantity of UCA1 transcripts is insufficient to disrupt hnRNP A1/p16INK binding
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that hnRNP A1 binds p16INK in proliferating cells where UCA1 levels are low.

claim: In proliferating cells, levels of p16INK mRNA are low due to direct repression by CAPERα/TBX3 and p16INK mRNA instability conferred by hnRNP A1.
source: and levels of p16INK mRNA are low due to: (1) direct repression by CAPERα/TBX3 and, (2) p16INK mRNA instability conferred by hnRNP A1.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective data showing CAPERα/TBX3 binding to p16INK regulatory elements and hnRNP A1-mediated destabilization of p16INK mRNA.

claim: When UCA1 levels increase during OIS, UCA1 binds and sequesters hnRNP A1, preventing it from destabilizing p16INK mRNA.
source: When UCA1 levels increase during OIS, by UCA1 overexpression, or via KD of CAPERα/TBX3, UCA1 binds and sequesters hnRNP A1, preventing it from destabilizing p16INK mRNA.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective data showing that increased UCA1 disrupts hnRNP A1/p16INK binding and stabilizes p16INK mRNA.

claim: CDKN2A-p16INK genomic regulatory elements bound in presenescent HFFs are not occupied by either TBX3 or CAPERα in RAS HFFs.
source: Increased p16 protein is required for RAS-induced senescence in MEFS and some human cell types (Serrano et al., 1997), leading us to determine whether OIS affects CAPERα/TBX3 occupancy of p16INK chromatin. CDKN2A-p16INK genomic regulatory elements bound in PS HFFs (Figure 4I) were not occupied by either TBX3 or CAPERα in RAS HFFs (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Chromatin marks on CDKN2A-p16INK regulatory elements switch from heterochromatic to euchromatic in RAS HFFs.
source: Chromatin marks on these regions switched from heterochromatic to euchromatic (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Chromatin marks on UCA1/A3 switch from heterochromatic to euchromatic in RAS HFFs.
source: This was also observed with UCA1/A3 (Figure 5U) and DUSP4 chromatin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 5U.

claim: Chromatin marks on DUSP4 regulatory elements switch from heterochromatic to euchromatic in RAS HFFs.
source: This was also observed with UCA1/A3 (Figure 5U) and DUSP4 chromatin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both TBX3 and CAPERα protein levels are increased in RAS HFFs compared to presenescent HFFs.
source: Surprisingly, both TBX3 and CAPERα protein levels were increased in RAS HFFs (Figure 7C)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TBX3 and CAPERα no longer co-immunoprecipitate in RAS HFFs.
source: but they no longer co-IP'd (Figure 7D, red box).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In RAS HFFs, CAPERα immunoreactivity becomes concentrated in large intranuclear foci.
source: Immunocytochemistry of endogenous TBX3 and CAPERα in PS and RAS HFFs confirmed increased protein levels in OIS (Figure 7F–M), and revealed dramatic changes in CAPERα localization: CAPERα immunoreactivity became concentrated in large intranuclear foci (Figure 7L,M)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figures 7L and 7M.

claim: CAPERα-positive intranuclear foci in RAS HFFs are distinct from SAHFs and PML bodies.
source: These foci are distinct from SAHFs and PML bodies (Figure 7M and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 7M and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: More than half of the transcripts with expression altered 1.5-fold or more by CAPERα knockdown are similarly affected by loss of TBX3.
source: More than half of the transcripts with expression altered 1.5-fold or more by CAPERα KD were similarly affected by loss of TBX3 (N = 2375 CAPERα KD, 2188 TBX3 KD; 1157 co-regulated, p<<<<0.0001, Figure 7—source data 1–3, Figure 7N,O).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7N and 7O and source data files.

claim: Gene ontology-biologic process analysis shows highly significant co-regulation of 'transcription regulation' transcripts (increased expression) by CAPERα and TBX3.
source: Gene ontology-biologic process (GO-BP) analysis with DAVID (Huang da et al., 2009a, 2009b) showed highly significant co-regulation of 'transcription regulation' (increased expression) and 'cell-cycle' (decreased expression) transcripts (Figure 7N,O).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-BP analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7N.

claim: Gene ontology-biologic process analysis shows highly significant co-regulation of 'cell-cycle' transcripts (decreased expression) by CAPERα and TBX3.
source: Gene ontology-biologic process (GO-BP) analysis with DAVID (Huang da et al., 2009a, 2009b) showed highly significant co-regulation of 'transcription regulation' (increased expression) and 'cell-cycle' (decreased expression) transcripts (Figure 7N,O).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-BP analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7O.

claim: IL6 is a direct target of CAPERα/TBX3.
source: Further interrogation of this group revealed that IL6 and HDAC9 are CAPERα/TBX3 direct targets and their upregulation in RAS is associated with loss of CAPERα/TBX3 binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: HDAC9 is a direct target of CAPERα/TBX3.
source: Further interrogation of this group revealed that IL6 and HDAC9 are CAPERα/TBX3 direct targets and their upregulation in RAS is associated with loss of CAPERα/TBX3 binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: 11% of CAPERα/TBX3 up-regulated transcripts are also increased by RAS.
source: We compared CAPERα/TBX3 co-regulated transcripts to a published data set comparing PS and G12VRAS fibroblasts (Loayza-Puch et al., 2013). This revealed that 11% of CAPERα/TBX3 up-regulated transcripts were also increased by RAS (Figure 7N′)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-Seq data with published data, shown in Figure 7N′.

claim: Among CAPERα/TBX3 and RAS co-upregulated transcripts, GO-BP 'programmed cell death' (31%) and 'transcription regulation' (34%) are highly overrepresented.
source: among these, GO-BP 'programmed cell death' (31%) and 'transcription regulation' (34%) were highly overrepresented.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-BP analysis shown in Figure 7N′.

claim: 30% of CAPERα/TBX3 down-regulated transcripts are also in the RAS data set.
source: 30% of CAPERα/TBX3 down-regulated transcripts were also in the RAS data set
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-Seq data with published data, shown in Figure 7O′.

claim: Among CAPERα/TBX3 and RAS co-downregulated transcripts, more than one-third are cell cycle genes.
source: >1/3 of these were cell cycle genes (Figure 7O′).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-BP analysis shown in Figure 7O′.

claim: In all comparisons of CAPERα/TBX3 and RAS transcriptional data, the number of transcripts common to both groups was greater than predicted by chance and highly statistically significant.
source: In all comparisons, the number of transcripts common to both groups was greater than predicted by chance and highly statistically significant (Figure 7—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypergeometric test results shown in Figure 7—source data 3.

claim: KEGG pathway analyses revealed overrepresented pathways that were common to both CAPERα/TBX3 and RAS data sets.
source: KEGG pathway analyses revealed overrepresented pathways that were common to both CAPERα/TBX3 and RAS data sets (Figure 7N–O′, pie charts)
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 7N-O′.

claim: JAK/STAT, TLR and TGFβ signaling pathways are significantly overrepresented in the CAPERα/TBX3 upregulated data set but not in the RAS upregulated data set.
source: but notably fewer pathways were shared in the upregulated group: JAK/STAT, TLR and TGFβ signaling pathways were only significantly overrepresented in the CAPERα/TBX3 data set.
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 7N′.
